exemplar: Douglass argues that the Fourth of July is a mockery to the enslaved: a celebration of liberty that exposes, by contrast, the cruelty and hypocrisy of a nation that holds millions in bondage.
The Compromise of 1850, especially the strengthened Fugitive Slave Act that forced Northerners to aid in capturing freedom seekers, deepened the sectional crisis Douglass describes.

The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) answered Douglass's indictment by destroying slavery as a legal institution and beginning to align American practice with its stated ideals.
parts: A. Briefly describe Douglass's view of the Fourth of July as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE development of the 1850s that deepened the sectional conflict Douglass describes.
C. Briefly explain ONE development of the 1860s that addressed Douglass's indictment of American slavery.

stimulus.attribution: Frederick Douglass, 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' Rochester, New York, July 5, 1852.
stimulus.text: What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.

exemplar: The photograph conveys that the Cold War's division of Europe collapsed from below: ordinary people, not diplomats, physically dismantling the wall that symbolized Soviet domination of the East.
Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) and his refusal to use Soviet force to hold the Eastern bloc together allowed East Germans to push through the border in November 1989.

The Cold War's end left the United States as the world's sole superpower, encouraging American-led interventions such as the Gulf War (1991) and debates over whether the U.S. should act as the world's policeman.
parts: A. Briefly describe what the photograph conveys about the end of the Cold War in Europe.
B. Briefly explain ONE development that contributed to the events shown in the photograph.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of these events for the role of the United States in the world.
items.pd_rationale: Photograph of the fall of the Berlin Wall, November 1989; verified on Wikimedia Commons (reproduction from public documentation). Coordinator to confirm license tag.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the 1989 photograph of crowds at the Berlin Wall (Wikimedia Commons).
stimulus.text: The photograph shows crowds of East and West Berliners standing and sitting atop the concrete Berlin Wall in November 1989, some waving, some hammering at the barrier. Behind them the Brandenburg Gate is visible. The mood is jubilant and chaotic - a physical wall being dismantled by the people it divided.
